transcript.text: Scarcity
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-01
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
WATCH OUT
Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING BETWEEN SCARCE USES

A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
CHECK YOURSELF
A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Incentives
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-02
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Predict behavioral responses and unintended consequences created by incentives.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Incentives change the expected benefits or costs of a choice, so they can alter behavior at the margin. A congestion fee raises the cost of the next downtown trip. Incentives can be monetary or nonmonetary, and different people may respond differently. A reward can also improve a measured result while harming the underlying goal.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A toll changes the cost of driving and can change travel choices.
A reward raises the benefit of an action, even when the reward is not money.
A policy can change behavior in unintended ways; consider the incentives it creates.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to define incentives as cash payments or guaranteed behavior. An incentive changes the expected payoff to a choice; it may be monetary or nonmonetary, and people can respond differently.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RESPONDING TO INCENTIVES

A city adds a $4 congestion fee for a rush-hour trip. Assume other trip costs are already deducted from each driver's benefit. A driver with a remaining benefit of $3 avoids the trip because the fee exceeds that benefit. A commuter with a remaining benefit of $10 still travels. The fee changes choices at the margin without making every driver respond alike.
CHECK YOURSELF
A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Opportunity Cost
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-03
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify and calculate the value of the next-best alternative.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made. Scarcity makes opportunity cost unavoidable because using time, money, or resources for one purpose prevents their use elsewhere. The cost is the single best forgone option, valued from the decision maker's perspective, and it can be monetary or nonmonetary.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a choice between two or more alternatives under a time, money, or resource constraint.
Identify the next-best alternative that the decision maker gives up.
Value the forgone alternative from the decision maker's perspective.
Do not add every rejected option; opportunity cost is the single best alternative forgone.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to add the value of every forgone option. Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING THE NEXT-BEST OPTION

A student can spend Saturday working for $80, studying for an exam worth an estimated $60 benefit, or attending a concert valued at $40. If the student studies, the best forgone alternative is the $80 work shift. The opportunity cost of studying is therefore $80, not $120 and not the concert's $40 value.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can spending an hour in a free park have an opportunity cost?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Marginal Analysis
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-04
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use marginal benefits and costs while avoiding sunk-cost reasoning.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit of the next unit or small change with its additional cost. A decision should expand while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost and stop before the next unit costs more than it adds. Sunk costs do not affect this forward-looking comparison, while costs or benefits imposed on others matter in social marginal analysis.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a decision about one more unit, one more hour, or a small change in an activity.
Compare the additional benefit of that change with its additional cost.
Continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost; stop before the next unit costs more than it adds.
Ignore totals or averages when the question asks whether the next unit is worthwhile.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to decide from total benefit or total cost. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost of the next unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPARING MARGINAL BENEFIT AND COST

A warehouse earns $15 from handling one additional box, and the marginal cost of that box is $13. Marginal net benefit is $15 - $13 = $2, so handling the box increases profit. If the next box cost $17 instead, its marginal net benefit would be -$2 and the warehouse should stop before that box.
CHECK YOURSELF
Total cost is $100 for 10 units, and producing an eleventh unit adds $15. Which number is average cost, and which is marginal cost?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-05
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish microeconomic and macroeconomic questions.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, workers, and individual markets. Macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment. One event can require both kinds of analysis. The distinction is the unit of analysis, not the size of an organization or dataset.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A report tracks national inflation, unemployment, and total output.
Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.
A bakery studies how customers respond to a muffin price increase.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to label any large organization as macroeconomic. The classification depends on the unit of analysis: one decision-maker is micro; economy-wide aggregates are macro.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MICRO OR MACRO?

A restaurant deciding whether to hire one more server is a microeconomic question because it concerns one firm's choice. The national unemployment rate is a macroeconomic outcome because it aggregates labor-market conditions across the economy. The subject's size is not decisive; the unit of analysis is.
CHECK YOURSELF
A national retailer studies how its own customers respond to a price increase. Is that question microeconomic or macroeconomic, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Positive vs. Normative Analysis
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-06
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Positive analysis makes claims that evidence can test, while normative analysis applies value judgments about what should be done. Identify what observation could support or contradict a testable claim. A positive claim can be false. A normative claim ranks goals or outcomes using values; evidence can inform that judgment but cannot settle the values alone.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership.
Ridership data can test the prediction even if it turns out to be wrong.
A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair.
A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat positive as good, true, or politically neutral. A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.
WORKED EXAMPLE: POSITIVE OR NORMATIVE?

The statement 'A lower bus fare will increase ridership' is positive because ridership data can support or contradict it. The statement 'The city should lower bus fares because access is fair' is normative because it applies a value judgment. Evidence can inform both statements, but only the first is directly testable as written.
CHECK YOURSELF
Is every policy statement normative?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Models and Assumptions
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-07
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Evaluate the purpose, assumptions, simplifications, and limits of economic models.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Economic models simplify reality to isolate the relationships that matter for a particular question. The two-good abstraction exposes scarcity and opportunity cost without describing every output. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context. Extra complexity is useful only when its benefits exceed lost clarity or robustness. Apply a model where its important assumptions remain reasonable.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Adding dozens of variables improves historical fit but makes the mechanism impossible to interpret.
A central bank changes its policy rule, and a forecasting relationship estimated under the old rule breaks down.
A local haircut model omits exchange rates and global shipping.
An economist builds a simple two-market circular-flow model and leaves out banks, government, and foreign trade.
An economist studies how price affects purchases while holding income constant.
WATCH OUT
Do not use the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A MODEL

A PPF model includes only two goods, even though real economies produce thousands. That simplification isolates scarcity and opportunity cost: moving toward more of one good requires less of the other. The model is useful for that purpose, but it would be inadequate for predicting the output of a specific industry without additional detail.
CHECK YOURSELF
What role does an assumption play in a model?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret PPF points, slopes, shifts, efficiency, growth, and opportunity cost.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A production possibilities frontier shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost: specialized resources become less well suited as production shifts toward the other good. Points inside indicate unused capacity; points outside are currently infeasible.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Points on the frontier use current resources efficiently; inside points leave capacity unused.
Using idle resources changes the production point, while resources or technology shift the frontier.
A bowed-out frontier indicates increasing opportunity cost.
WATCH OUT
Moving from inside to the frontier uses idle capacity. Moving the frontier outward requires more resources or better technology.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING A PPF

The horizontal axis is Good X and the vertical axis is Good Y. A bowed-out frontier passes through A at (0, 50), B at (8, 45), C at (15, 35), D at (21, 20), and E at (25, 0). F is inside the frontier near (8, 20), and G is outside it near (21, 48).

On the PPF, moving from point C (15 units of X and 35 of Y) to point D (21 of X and 20 of Y) gains 6 units of X but gives up 15 units of Y. The total opportunity cost is 15 units of Y, or 15/6 = 2.5 units of Y per additional unit of X.
CHECK YOURSELF
Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-09
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost, even when another producer has an absolute advantage in both goods. Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost. Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain. Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange. Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.
Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs.
One producer is more productive in both goods.
Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to choose the producer with the greatest absolute output. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, and a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade ratio lies between the two opportunity costs.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE

Ari gives up 24/12 = 2 rugs per lamp; Bea gives up 60/10 = 6 rugs per lamp. Ari has comparative advantage in lamps. For rugs, Bea gives up 1/6 lamp, below Ari's 1/2 lamp. A trade of one lamp for four rugs lies between the two lamp costs, so both can gain from specializing and exchanging.
CHECK YOURSELF
If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Economists and Policy
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-10
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Analyze the economist's role in policy advice.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Economists use evidence and models to estimate policy effects, identify tradeoffs, and explain uncertainty. Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences. Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal. Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments. Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption.
Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.
A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period.
Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to give economists authority to choose society's values. Economists can estimate consequences and tradeoffs; the policy choice also requires normative judgments.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING POLICY ADVICE

An economist estimates that a proposed transit subsidy will increase ridership by 8%, but the estimate comes from a city with denser development. Professional advice reports the predicted benefit, explains the uncertain transfer to the local setting, and identifies fiscal costs. Whether those consequences justify the policy also depends on public values and priorities.
CHECK YOURSELF
An estimate from a dense city predicts an 8% ridership gain in a rural area. Which assumption about travel alternatives should the economist examine before applying that estimate?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Competitive Markets
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-11
Time: 4 minutes
Outcome: Identify the conditions that create price-taking behavior and limited market power
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A competitive market contains many independent buyers and sellers, usually trading products that buyers view as close substitutes. No single participant controls enough of the market to set the market price. A small firm is therefore a price taker: it chooses how much to sell at the price created by market supply and demand. Competition becomes stronger when firms can enter or exit, buyers can compare offers, and switching among sellers is easy.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Many independent firms sell the same product or close substitutes.
One seller supplies only a small share of total market output.
A firm accepts a price determined by overall market supply and demand.
Buyers can compare prices and switch sellers without much difficulty.
Entry by new firms or exit by existing firms changes competitive pressure.
WATCH OUT

A market is not strictly competitive just because it has several sellers. Product differentiation, search costs, network effects, or barriers to entry can still give firms pricing power. The key question is whether one seller can raise its price persistently without losing many customers to available alternatives.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING A PRICE TAKER

A wheat farmer is one of thousands selling a standardized crop. The posted market price is $6 per bushel. If this farmer asks $7 while other farmers still charge $6, buyers can purchase identical wheat elsewhere. The farmer is too small to move the market price, so raising the price would sharply reduce sales. The evidence - many sellers, a standardized product, and easy switching - identifies price-taking behavior.
CHECK YOURSELF
An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare, but a merger leaves one company controlling most available inventory. Which fact strengthens competition, which fact weakens it, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Demand & the Law of Demand
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain demand, quantity demanded, and movements along a demand curve.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Demand describes the quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices, holding other demand conditions constant. Quantity demanded is the amount buyers choose at one particular price. The law of demand states that a lower own price increases quantity demanded and a higher own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same demand curve; it does not shift the curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The good's own price changes while income, tastes, expectations, related-good prices, and the number of buyers remain constant.
The question asks for quantity demanded at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same downward-sloping demand curve.
A lower price is paired with a larger quantity demanded.
WATCH OUT
A change in the good's own price moves along demand. Only a nonprice determinant shifts the demand curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MOVEMENT ALONG DEMAND

Price ($) is vertical; Quantity of gourmet donuts (thousands) is horizontal. A is 100 thousand donuts at $10; B is 225 thousand at $5. Both lie on one downward demand curve, so A to B increases quantity demanded by 125 thousand.

On the gourmet-donut graph, point A shows a price of $10 and quantity demanded of 100 thousand. Point B shows a lower price of $5 and quantity demanded of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same demand curve and only the good's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity demanded of 125 thousand, not an increase in demand.
CHECK YOURSELF
The price of a concert ticket falls and buyers move to another point on the same demand curve. What changes: demand or quantity demanded?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Determinants of Demand
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift demand left or right.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Demand shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Demand increases and shifts right when buyers want more at every price; demand decreases and shifts left when they want less at every price. Important determinants include income, tastes and preferences, expectations, the number of buyers, and the prices of substitutes and complements. The direction of an income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, and the effect of a related-good price depends on whether the goods are substitutes or complements.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Consumer income, preferences, expectations, or the number of buyers changes.
The price of a substitute or complement changes.
Quantity demanded changes at the same price.
The entire demand curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a demand shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A nonprice determinant changes how much buyers want at every price and shifts the entire curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DEMAND SHIFT
Price ($) is vertical; Quantity of coffee (thousands) is horizontal. At $10, D0 gives 50 thousand and D1 gives 125 thousand. D1 is a rightward demand shift at unchanged price.

At a coffee price of $10, the original curve D0 shows quantity demanded of 50 thousand, while D1 shows 125 thousand. The price of coffee is held constant, so the 75-thousand increase cannot be a movement along D0. It is a rightward shift from D0 to D1, meaning a nonprice determinant has increased demand.
CHECK YOURSELF
Income rises for buyers of a normal good. Which direction does its demand curve shift, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Supply & the Law of Supply
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-14
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain supply, quantity supplied, and movements along a supply curve.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Supply describes the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices, holding other supply conditions constant. Quantity supplied is the amount sellers offer at one particular price. The law of supply states that a higher own price generally increases quantity supplied and a lower own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same supply curve; it does not shift the curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The good's own price changes while production conditions remain constant.
The question asks for quantity supplied at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same upward-sloping supply curve.
A higher price is paired with a larger quantity supplied.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in supply. If the good's own price changes and sellers move from one point to another on the same supply curve, quantity supplied changes. Supply itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MOVEMENT ALONG SUPPLY
Price ($) is vertical; Quantity of coffee (thousands) is horizontal. A is 100 thousand at $6; B is 225 thousand at $11. Both lie on one upward supply curve, so this is movement along supply.

On the coffee supply graph, point A shows a price of $6 and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Point B shows a higher price of $11 and quantity supplied of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same supply curve and only coffee's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity supplied of 125 thousand, not an increase in supply.
CHECK YOURSELF
The market price of handmade tables rises and sellers move to another point on the same supply curve. What changes?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Determinants of Supply
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-15
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift supply left or right.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Supply shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Supply increases and shifts right when sellers can provide more at every price; supply decreases and shifts left when they provide less at every price. Important determinants include input and resource costs, technology and productivity, taxes and subsidies, expectations, the number of sellers, and natural or regulatory production conditions. A change that lowers marginal production cost generally increases supply, while a change that raises marginal cost generally decreases it.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Input prices, technology, productivity, taxes, or subsidies change.
Producers' expectations or the number of sellers changes.
Quantity supplied changes at the same price.
The entire supply curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a supply shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A change in production cost, technology, expectations, or the number of sellers changes how much firms offer at every price and shifts the curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SUPPLY SHIFT
Price ($) is vertical; Quantity of hamburgers (thousands) is horizontal. At $9, S0 gives 200 thousand and S1 gives 100 thousand. S1 is a leftward supply shift.

At a hamburger price of $9, the original curve S0 shows quantity supplied of 200 thousand, while S1 shows 100 thousand. The product's price is unchanged, so the 100-thousand decrease is not a movement along S0. It is a leftward shift from S0 to S1, consistent with a determinant such as higher input costs reducing supply.
CHECK YOURSELF
A new technology lowers the cost of producing solar panels. Which direction does supply shift, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Market Equilibrium
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price, buyers can purchase the amount they want and sellers can sell the amount they offer, so there is no pressure for price to change. A demand or supply shift creates a new intersection and can change both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
On a graph, use the intersection of the demand and supply curves.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage; a price above equilibrium creates a surplus.
Report both the equilibrium price and the corresponding equilibrium quantity.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to call any intersection or stated price an equilibrium. Equilibrium occurs only where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

Price in dollars is vertical; quantity in thousands is horizontal. Downward demand and upward supply intersect at E, quantity 150 and price 5. No curve shifts are shown. Above 5 supply exceeds demand; below 5 demand exceeds supply.

Demand and supply intersect at a price of $5 and quantity of 150 thousand. Buyers want exactly the amount sellers offer at that point. A price above $5 creates a surplus; a price below $5 creates a shortage. This example finds equilibrium without shifting either curve.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a price below $5 on this graph, which quantity is larger, and what pressure does that create on price?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Shortages and Surpluses
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-17
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. Buyers competing for limited supply put upward pressure on price. A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded; sellers then face pressure to lower price. Adjustment tends toward the price where the two quantities are equal.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
At $2 per gallon, buyers want 200 thousand gallons while sellers offer 100 thousand: a shortage.
Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus.
Compare quantities at the same price, then identify the pressure on price.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to reverse shortage and price pressure. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING A SHORTAGE

Gas quantity in thousands of gallons is horizontal; price per gallon is vertical. Demand slopes down, supply slopes up. Equilibrium E is at 150 thousand gallons and $3. At $2, demand is 200 thousand and supply 100 thousand: a shortage of 100 thousand, pushing price upward. At $4, demand is 100 thousand and supply 200 thousand: a surplus of 100 thousand, pushing price downward.

At a price of $2 per gallon, the graph shows quantity demanded of 200 thousand gallons and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Because buyers want 100 thousand more gallons than sellers offer, the market has a shortage of 200 - 100 = 100 thousand gallons. Upward pressure on price follows.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a price of $4, buyers want 100 thousand gallons and sellers offer 200 thousand. Calculate the imbalance and predict the pressure on price.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Simultaneous Shifts
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

When demand and supply shift at the same time, each shift contributes separately to the new equilibrium. Analyze how each change affects price and quantity, then combine the directional effects. If both shifts push one variable in the same direction, that result is determinate; if they push in opposite directions, the result depends on the relative size of the shifts.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Both a demand determinant and a supply determinant change.
A bicycle endorsement raises demand while higher input costs reduce supply.
Analyze each shift separately before combining its price and quantity effects.
Opposing effects on one variable leave its direction ambiguous unless relative shift sizes are known.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts. A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMBINING DEMAND AND SUPPLY SHIFTS

Price ($) is vertical; Gas (thousand gallons) is horizontal. D0 and S0 meet at quantity 150 and price 3. Demand right to D1 and supply left to S1 both raise price; in this equal-sized illustration the new intersection is quantity 150, price 5. Quantity need not be unchanged for other relative shift sizes.

The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 and quantity of 150 thousand. After demand shifts right to D1 and supply shifts left to S1, the new intersection is $5 and the same quantity of 150 thousand. Both shifts raise price; their opposing quantity effects happen to offset in this graph, though quantity would otherwise be ambiguous.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Price Ceilings
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-19
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding ceilings and analyze shortages and rationing.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price ceiling sets a legal maximum price and is binding only when it lies below the market equilibrium price. A binding ceiling keeps price from rising to equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage develops. A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the legal maximum price with the market equilibrium price.
A ceiling below equilibrium is binding and creates excess demand.
At the ceiling price, read quantity demanded and quantity supplied; their difference is the shortage.
A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to assume that every price ceiling is binding. A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BINDING PRICE CEILING

Price ($) is vertical; Quantity is horizontal. Demand and supply meet at quantity 200, price $30. At $20 demand is 250 and supply 150, a shortage of 100. At $40 demand is 150 and supply 250, a surplus of 100.

The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding ceiling of $20 holds price below equilibrium; buyers demand 250 units while sellers supply 150. The resulting shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some willing buyers cannot purchase at the controlled price.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a binding price ceiling, Qd = 90 and Qs = 60. What is the shortage?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Price Floors
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-20
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding floors and analyze surpluses and unintended effects.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A price floor sets a legal minimum price and is binding only when it lies above the market equilibrium price. A binding floor keeps price from falling to equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus develops. A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the legal minimum price with the market equilibrium price.
A floor above equilibrium is binding and creates excess supply.
At the floor price, read quantity supplied and quantity demanded; their difference is the surplus.
